kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.manufacturer: generic; no single named manufacturer confirmed. MB102 is a widely cloned reference design produced by many OEMs
identity.manufacturer_part_number: MB102 (de facto standard model designation used industry-wide)
generic_equivalents: any "MB102" or "MB-102" breadboard power supply module
identity.package: module (small PCB that clips onto the end power rails of an 830-point breadboard)

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A little board that turns a 9V battery or wall adapter into clean, steady 5V and 3.3V power for your breadboard circuits.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Powering breadboard circuits without needing the Uno or a USB cable connected; useful when you want a project to run on its own.
function.how_it_works_briefly: It takes power in through a barrel jack or USB port, then uses onboard voltage regulators to produce steady 3.3V and 5V outputs, feeding them out to the breadboard's power rails through two pairs of pins that you select with small jumpers.

pinout.name: GND
pinout.notes: 4-pin header group; ground return, connects to the breadboard's negative rails

pinout.name: Left jumper
pinout.notes: Selects that side's rail voltage: 5V / OFF (0V) / 3.3V

pinout.name: Right jumper
pinout.notes: Selects that side's rail voltage: 5V / OFF (0V) / 3.3V

pinout.name: ON/OFF switch
pinout.notes: Cuts power to the whole board

pins.pin_1_identification: No single pin 1. The board is a rectangle with two independent output pin clusters, one on each long edge, mirrored around a center barrel jack and switch. Each side's polarity is silkscreened (+ / -) right next to its pins.

electrical.operating_voltage: 3.3V or 5V selectable output per side, via jumper
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: 12V max input (per the sources' rated 6.5-12V input range; exceeding this risks damaging the onboard regulator, though no source stated a hard absolute maximum separate from the recommended range)
electrical.typical_current: well under the 700 mA max in typical breadboard projects (LEDs, small sensors)
electrical.logic_level: n/a (power supply, not a logic device)

key_specs.output_voltage_options: 5V, 3.3V, or 0V/off, independently per side via jumper
key_specs.connectors: 5.5x2.1mm DC barrel jack, USB Type-A input, ON/OFF switch, power-on indicator LED

visual_identification.shape_and_size: A small rectangular PCB, about 5.3cm x 3.3cm, with two rows of pin headers along its long edges spaced to plug straight into a standard breadboard's end power rails, and a round barrel jack plus a USB-A port sticking out one end.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Usually a blue PCB with white silkscreen; two small black switches near the middle for jumper voltage selection; a small LED that lights when powered.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: Silkscreen near the header pins usually reads "5V", "3.3V", and "GND" or +/- symbols, plus "MB102" printed on the board.
easily_confused_with: A generic USB charging module (no barrel jack or breadboard-pin footprint)
A relay module (similar size, but has a large relay can and screw terminals instead of breadboard pins)

example_connections.uno_pin: not wired to the Uno directly; plugs straight into the breadboard's own power rail holes
share a common ground with the Uno only if both are powering the same circuit at the same time

required_extra_parts: 9V battery or a 6.5-12V wall adapter with a compatible barrel plug
830-point breadboard (this module clips onto its end rails)
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none; it is a passive power module, no code needed

hazards: Reversed barrel-jack polarity can damage the module
Setting both jumpers to 5V while a 3.3V-only part is wired in can destroy that part
Shorting the output rails together can overheat the regulator
handling_notes: Turn the switch off before changing the jumpers or rewiring the breadboard
Double check jumper position before powering anything sensitive
common_mistakes: Leaving a jumper in the wrong voltage position for the parts wired to that rail
Plugging the module onto the breadboard backwards (check the printed +/- markings line up with the breadboard's own rail markings)
Forgetting to flip the ON/OFF switch and assuming the module is broken

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: No power on the breadboard rails
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Switch is off, a jumper is set to the middle OFF position, or no input power is connected
symptoms_and_causes.check: Verify the ON/OFF switch position and that both jumpers are set to 5V or 3.3V, not the middle

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Jumper set to 5V when the circuit needs 3.3V, or reversed barrel-jack polarity
symptoms_and_causes.check: Measure the actual rail voltage with a multimeter before reconnecting parts

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With input power connected and the switch on, measure DC volts between the output + and - pins on each side; expect close to 5.0V or 3.3V depending on that side's jumper position.

confidence.notes: MB102 is a generic, multi-sourced reference design with no single manufacturer datasheet. All specs are corroborated across two independent retailer/tutorial pages that agree with each other (6.5-12V in, 700 mA max, 5V/3.3V/off per side).
